accuracy.evidence: Matches the topic's description and evidence statements: listening to a short story to the end (four-page Kit the cat story whose answer is only on the last page), staying with a puzzle (three-piece fish), and returning to an activity after a distraction (bird, beeping TV, barking dog) with adult help (challenge 'A grown-up can help me'). Claims in the adult text were checked: background TV shortens and fragments toddler toy play (Schmidt, Pempek, Kirkorian, Lund and Anderson 2008, Child Development), and fewer toys led toddlers to play longer with each toy (Dauch, Imwalle, Ocasio and Metz 2018, Infant Behavior and Development). No fixed minutes-per-year rule is stated, since that rule of thumb is not well evidenced; the text says only a few minutes.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real beliefs and adult habits behind weak early attention: that one look away ends the activity (puzzle prediction, challenge 'over', m4 'Yes, I am naughty'), that switching between many things gets more done (challenge 'all' and 'fast'), that the end of a story can be known without listening on (story prediction, wrong answers bed and box), that noise and clutter do not matter (calm-room prediction, 'TV on loud' and 'Lots of toys out' in the sorter), and that there is no way back once lost (challenge 'Nobody can').

lab_distinct.evidence: Every mechanic is built around a distraction and a return: the cup tower refuses new cups while the bird card is being watched until 'Look back at my cups' is pressed; the story pauses on a beeping TV and the final question can only be answered after the last page; the fish puzzle pauses on a bark and offers stop or look back; a room of noisy things must be dragged into a toy box while the puzzle is kept; and one duck moves among changing shiny pictures. None of it could be relabelled for another topic; the distinctness gate passed against all flagship labs, including flagtry (persisting) and flaglisten.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers the idea by acting: watching the bird visibly stops the tower at two cups and looking back makes it grow again; stopping at page 2 leaves bed and box as tempting wrong answers that the last page disproves; after the bark, choosing Stop shows 'The puzzle is not over' and choosing look back finishes the fish; clearing four things leaves 'Just the puzzle now. Nice and calm.' Each finished task names the idea: the tower only grew while your eyes were on the cups; looking away is OK, coming back finished the fish.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'A bird flies by. What helps you finish? Watch the bird / Look back at the cups' (watching freezes the tower), 'Can you tell where the ball is if you stop at page 2? Yes / No' (pages 2 and 3 say No ball!), 'You looked away from the puzzle. Is it over? Yes / No, I can come back' (Stop is answered with 'The puzzle is not over'), and 'Where is it easier to do a puzzle? With the TV on and lots of toys / With just the puzzle'.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with rotated answer order and a streak count; every wrong answer names the slip: 'The toy pulls you away, and you miss the end', 'It is not over! Looking away is OK', 'Loud noise pulls your eyes and ears away. A quiet spot helps', 'Doing it all at once means nothing gets finished', 'Jumping between things is slower', 'Talking over the story means you miss the words. Breathe, then listen', 'Grown-ups can help you come back'.

readability.evidence: Kid text is FK grade -0.7 (family limit 5.0) with short sentences of everyday words (pick one thing, look back, keep going); adult text is FK 9.6 (limit 10.0). Lab lines are short, one idea per screen, with big pictures (cups drawn in five colours, a cat story with one emoji per page, a fish built from three coloured shapes, a duck among shiny things), so an adult can read aloud to a pre-reader.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs each carry one move: pick one thing and stay, looking away is OK so look back, stopping means missing the end, and clear away extra things. Adult paragraphs give what the skill is at this age, what each lab step does, named mistakes backed by two studies, and a concrete way to invite a child back. The sorter (helps me stay / pulls me away) is not a copy of any lab step.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of every step plus mid-task shots (bird distraction, story page 3, fish after the bark, room part-cleared). Fixed two problems seen in the shots: the 'Put away' counter overlapped the toy box, so the toy box moved to the bottom row and the counter to the top; and the add-piece card now shows the piece's shape beside its label. Cards are at least about 64 px tall and the phone sweep reported 0 findings.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Stack a cup, Look at the bird, Look back at my cups, Next page, Watch the TV, Back to the story, each answer, Add the tail/body/head, Stop or Look back, put away each item, and a picture-labelled button for each of the six duck boxes). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action, e.g. 'Tower: 2 of 5 cups. A bird is flying by.' and 'Find the duck. Boxes: duck, star, present, sparkle, kite, balloon.' Challenge feedback is a polite live region with a text tick or cross, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) was clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
